text:
I worked at microcenter. 
I spoke on average with over 20-40 people a day. 

Almost no one uses ray tracing. It's the most overrated, oversaturated argument 
I've heard yet in the PC gaming market. 
In fact, even the 4090 often needs DLSS to do proper 4k 60+ depending on the title.
Speaking of which, there is like 2-3 games relevant that even use ray tracing. And even still people with a 4090 turn it off to enjoy better response time, and higher framerates. 

From my actual experience with customers who use these products. 
I have learned quite allot. 
People get the card, they turn on DLSS+FG and max RT they say "cool" 
and then turn it back off, right back off. 

So yeah, I recommend anyone to get the 7900 xt over the 4070 ti super. It not only is stronger overall, it's also competitive at nanite from unreal 5 (better way of "ray tracing" if you will) 
20gb of ram, and higher 1% lows, and better frametimes as well.

The micro stutter issue from Vsync and just in general is still there despiote Nvidia addressing it with driver ipdates.

Other than ray tracing, (and in some games DLSS), and that really only applies to the high-end cards, there's really no benefit for the regular gamer to go with Nvidia. If you're waiting for the 5000 series and think that the price is going to be fairer, you don't know Nvidia. I'm not saying that AMD are angels or anything, but there are a couple of good sensible options at a high price, but at least not insultingly high for what they give you. Interestingly, the original price for the 4090 was not that off the line, considering how insanely that thing was built. But every single card going down from that halo product, has been 40% too high, with the super models being generally $200 too high, though I would think that the TI is about $300 too high, given that it's basically giving 16 GB finally. Actually that 16 GB is exactly why I think it's still a problem, no $600 plus card should have anything less than 20 GB... This is Nvidia giving you planned obsolescence in these cards at eye watering prices, they want you to replace your card every 2 years even if you've paid $800 or more

text:
Steve, 7900 XTX owner here. I think the Radeon should be 10% cheaper is a little bit simplistic. When you have more than adequate rasterization performance on both GPUs, even with a slightly advantage in the Radeon side this becomes mostly irrelevant compared to having OK RT performance on all tested games on Nvidia side vs unplayable performance on some tested games on the Radeon side.

In other words, if rasterization is a non-issue, more and more the price difference will be determined by RT performance, and to a lesser extent, longevity due to VRAM size), as 16GB vs. 20GB is less of an issue than 12GB vs. 16GB at least for now. It will very likely that when 16GB is not enough, developers will start optimizing for 24GB (and not 20GB) as there are way more 24GB cards out there than 20GB. 

In the beginning I said simplistic because, if purely for gaming, I’d take a 4070Ti Super over a 7900 XT and in some cases, even over a 7900 XTX just for RT and DLSS in most scenarios.

@Boorock70  $110, as the price difference is here, is my monthly electricity bill (base subscription removed). My energy bill includes a washing machine (2kW), tumble dryer (700w), dishwasher (1.2kW), kettle (2.4kW) and induction stove and oven (3.6kW). 40-60W is BUGGER ALL in a household. 

If we go with $0.50/kWh and a 60W deficit that turns out to $0.03 per hour. With a $110 price difference that is 3,666 of gaming before break-even. Even when playing 8 hours a day (the perks of still living with mummy and daddy) that is 458 days or 15 months (and 15 pay checks to take care of it!) before break even. For somewhat realistic gaming hours it translates to: break-even when the product is at retirement age. So I'm going to be a bit rude here and say "Please use a calculator/spread-sheet before you open your mouth."

My XTX at home runs 3x1440p@165Hz and uses 45W when running a youtube video in full-screen on one monitor.

My RTX Quadro at work runs 3x4K@120Hz and uses 35W when running a youtube video in full-screen on one monitor.

text:
@srobeck77 RT isn't even a concern for the lower end cards considering they can't even run RT or Path Tracing at even 1080p native, by the time 5000 series comes around Nvidia will release Super Path Tracing with DLSS4.0 Super downscaling and your 4000 series GPU will be obsolete (Example). Not even the 4090 can run Cyberpunk Path Tracing 1440p at 60FPS without upscaling from 1080p which is what DLSS quality is on a 1440p panel so you are paying $2000USD to play at 1080p on a 1440p panel or 1440p on a 4k panel (DLSS quality). In Straight Path Tracing the 4090 can't even hit 35FPS at 1440p without redering from a lower resolution. 

Reviewers along with Nvidia have convinced the top 1% that RT and DLSS is THE selling point when none can even do it without downscaling, this should tell you that we are many many years away from 4k 144hz Path Tracing or even 1440p 144hz. The top RTX GPU on Steam is the RTX3060 and that's not even the 12gb version, the market has spoken. 0.75% of Steam users own 4080's and 4090 owners are less than that at 0.45%, till Nvidia or AMD release a $300 card that can do Path Tracing at 1080p without downscaling Path Tracing and RT will never be adopted by the majority. 

This is the 3rd generation of RT and the only card adopted on mass is the RTX3060 at 5% according to Steam hardware survey, as I said the market has spoken and RT is years off from being adopted by the majority and I don't see Nvidia or AMD offering a GPU for $300 that can do this considering GPU's are getting more expensive with each generation which further decreases adoption of the features they offer. 

This is reality. Anybody that can afford a 4080 or 4090 bought one and the rest of the majority cannot afford RT or simply don't think its an important factor in their purchasing decision. FSR and DLSS is the most interesting part for the majority since it increases the life span of their purchase but Nvidia has even locked future interations of DLSS to new generations, majority of people do not like that. 

This is why RT is good enough on Radeon 7000 series, Nvidia 3000 series RT performance with better raster across their offerings (Excluding the 4090) is good enough for the majority. I've recommended the 6700XT and 7800XT to friends over the RTX4060, 4070, 4070S, 4070TiS and the 7900XT and XTX over the 4080, these cards run our games perfectly fine and were significantly cheaper even considered actually affordable..

When you watch an RTX4080 or 4090 review you get the perspective of a 4080, 4090 owner but in the real world the majority of people can't even run RT even with downscaling, you make the mistake of over estimating the importance of RT to majority of gamers. It simply does not matter to the majority because its not finanacially feasible.

I own a both Intel and AMD processors also Nvidia and Radeon cards, Radeon offers value well more value than Nvidia and Nvidia's features just don't matter to the majority of people. Maybe in 5 years? Things might change but given the prices I highly doubt it.

text: ​ @markthompson4567  more cache, cores and memory at the same tdp does not mean more performance. All the resources are competing for the cards power. This card will definitely overclock better but the main performance uplift is the cores and a roughly 7% increase for for 10% more cores at that power profile is about right. Cores don't scale linearly with performance in gaming, otherwise the 4090 would be actually double this card, which it isn't (though it isn't too far off sometimes). The review is sloppy, but the outcome is pretty accurate. Cache, memory and bandwidth don't improve performance, they only limit performance if they aren't good enough.
